title: Tabular Representation and Summary Statistics of One Categorical Variable
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 1.3 Tabular Representation and Summary Statistics of One Categorical Variable
intro: Construct frequency and relative frequency tables and support categorical claims with counts and proportions.

moments.title: Frequency tables
moments.text: A frequency is the number of observations in a category.

moments.title: Relative frequency tables
moments.text: Divide each category count by the total.

moments.title: Proportions and percentages
moments.text: Multiply a proportion by 100 to express it as a percentage.

moments.title: Rounding
moments.text: Retain enough precision to interpret the data.

moments.title: Describe the table
moments.text: Identify common categories and compare their counts or proportions.

moments.title: Lemur types
moments.text: Count each lemur type to organize the sample.

moments.title: Calculate relative frequencies
moments.text: The sample contains 70 lemurs, including 20 ring-tailed and 11 mouse lemurs.

moments.title: Most common category
moments.text: Compare the counts to identify the modal category.

cards.name: Frequency
cards.text: A category count answers how many.

cards.name: Relative frequency
cards.text: The category count divided by the total answers what proportion.

cards.name: Percentage
cards.text: A relative frequency expressed out of 100.

cards.name: Check the total
cards.text: Mutually exclusive, exhaustive category counts total the sample size.

questions.q: In the video's sample of 70 lemurs, 20 are ring-tailed and 11 are mouse lemurs. Find each relative frequency.

steps.t: Use the full sample as the denominator.

work.text: Both proportions use the total of 70 lemurs.

steps.t: Divide each category count by the total.

work.text: Keep the unrounded fractions for calculations.

questions.answer: About 28.6% of the sampled lemurs are ring-tailed and 15.7% are mouse lemurs.

traps.title: Counts do not change variable type
traps.weak: Lemur type becomes quantitative after counting.
traps.better: Lemur type remains categorical; the table records counts of each type.

traps.title: Wrong denominator
traps.better: Divide by the total number of observations in the relevant sample.

traps.title: Rounded totals
traps.weak: Rounded percentages must sum to exactly 100%.
traps.better: Unrounded relative frequencies sum to 1. Rounded displays can differ slightly.

questions.stem: A survey records walking: 18, cycling: 12, bus: 30. What is the relative frequency for cycling?
why: 12/30 uses the bus count, not the total.

questions.stem: A pet-type table gives 38% dogs, 27% cats, 21% fish, and 14% other. Which claim is supported?
opts: Dogs are 38% of all pets in the country
Dogs are the most common recorded category
why: These data do not establish a country-wide percentage.
38% exceeds each of the other category percentages.

questions.stem: A relative frequency table totals 0.999 after rounding. What is the best response?
opts: Check the counts and rounding before declaring an error
Add an observation to the largest category
Replace the last proportion with zero
why: Small discrepancies can result from rounding.
Changing data is not a valid correction.
Rounding does not determine variable type.

questions.stem: Which is sufficient to recover category counts exactly from relative frequencies?
opts: The total and exact, unrounded proportions
why: A percentage alone does not determine a count.
The variable name supplies no sample size.
Multiply each exact proportion by the total.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: A community center records one preferred activity for each of 80 members: swimming 32, badminton 24, yoga 16, and other 8.
parts: (a) Construct a frequency and relative frequency table in words or text.
(b) Describe the two most common preferences using percentages.
(c) Assess the claim that a majority chose swimming.
sample: (a) Swimming: 32, 0.40; badminton: 24, 0.30; yoga: 16, 0.20; other: 8, 0.10. Counts total 80 and proportions total 1.
(b) Swimming is most common at 40%, followed by badminton at 30%.
(c) The claim is false: 40% chose swimming, which is less than 50%. It is the largest category, but not a majority.
checklist: Gives all four correct relative frequencies.
Compares the two largest categories in context.
Distinguishes a modal category from a majority.
